paragraphs: She was sitting in the kitchen with her grandmother, and the two of them were about to go to bed. They trusted Nazar Ivanovitch and hadn’t locked the door. Mitya ran in, pounced on Fenya and seized her by the throat.
“Tell me now! Where is she? Who is she with at Mokroe?” he roared furiously.
Both women screamed.
“Aie! I’ll tell you! Aie! Dmitri Fyodorovitch, darling, I’ll tell you everything this minute, I won’t hide anything,” Fenya gabbled, frightened to death. “She’s gone to Mokroe, to her officer.”
“What officer?” roared Mitya.
“Her officer, the one she used to know, the one who threw her over five years ago,” Fenya cackled, as fast as she could get the words out.

Mitya took away the hands that were squeezing her throat. He stood facing her, pale as death and unable to say a word, but his eyes showed that he understood it all, all of it, from the first word, and had guessed the whole situation. Poor Fenya was in no state just then to notice whether he understood or not. She stayed sitting on the trunk where she had been when he ran in, trembling all over, holding her hands out in front of her as if to protect herself. She seemed to have gone rigid in that position. Her wide, frightened eyes were fixed on him without moving. And to make matters worse, both his hands were smeared with blood. He must have touched his forehead with them on the way, as he ran, wiping off the sweat, so there were bloodstained patches on his forehead and his right cheek. Fenya was on the verge of hysterics. The old cook had jumped up and was staring at him like a madwoman, almost unconscious with terror.

Mitya stood for a moment, then sank mechanically onto a chair next to Fenya. He sat there, not thinking, but stunned, as if numbed by terror. Yet everything was as clear as day. That officer: he knew about him, he knew everything perfectly well. He had heard it from Grushenka herself, and had known that a letter had come from the man a month ago. So for a month, a whole month, this had been going on behind his back, right up to the arrival of this new man, and he had never given him a thought! But how could he, how could he not have thought of him? Why had he forgotten this officer, just like that, forgotten him as soon as he heard of him? That was the question that stood before him like some monstrous thing. And he looked at this monstrous thing with horror, growing cold with horror.

But suddenly, as gently and mildly as a sweet, affectionate child, he began speaking to Fenya as if he had completely forgotten how he had just frightened and hurt her. He started questioning her with an extreme precision that was astonishing in his state. And though the girl kept staring wildly at his bloodstained hands, she too answered every question with remarkable readiness and speed, as if she were eager to lay the whole truth and nothing but the truth before him. Little by little, even with a kind of enjoyment, she began explaining every detail. She didn’t want to torment him, but seemed eager to be of the greatest possible use to him. She described the whole of that day in great detail: the visit from Rakitin and Alyosha, how she, Fenya, had stood watch, how her mistress had set off, and how she had called out of the window to Alyosha, telling him to give Mitya her greetings and tell him “to remember for ever how she had loved him for an hour.”
When he heard about the message, Mitya suddenly smiled, and a flush of color came into his pale cheeks. At that moment Fenya said to him, not a bit afraid now to be inquisitive:
“Look at your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. They’re covered in blood!”
“Yes,” answered Mitya mechanically. He glanced carelessly at his hands and at once forgot them, and forgot Fenya’s question too.

He sank into silence again. Twenty minutes had passed since he ran in. His first horror was over, but clearly some new, fixed determination had taken hold of him. He suddenly stood up, smiling dreamily.
“What’s happened to you, sir?” said Fenya, pointing to his hands again. She spoke with pity, as if she felt very close to him now in his grief. Mitya looked at his hands again.

“That’s blood, Fenya,” he said, looking at her strangely. “That’s human blood, and, my God, why was it shed? But ... Fenya ... there’s a fence here” (he looked at her as if setting her a riddle), “a high fence, terrible to look at. But at dawn tomorrow, when the sun rises, Mitya will leap over that fence.... You don’t understand what fence, Fenya, and never mind.... You’ll hear tomorrow and understand ... and now, goodbye. I won’t stand in her way. I’ll step aside, I know how to step aside. Live, my joy.... You loved me for an hour, so remember Mityenka Karamazov for ever.... She always used to call me Mityenka, do you remember?”
And with those words he suddenly walked out of the kitchen. Fenya was almost more frightened by this sudden departure than she had been when he ran in and attacked her.

Just ten minutes later Dmitri went to see Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, the young official with whom he had pawned his pistols. It was already half-past eight. Pyotr Ilyitch had finished his evening tea and had just put his coat on again to go to the “Metropolis” to play billiards. Mitya caught him as he was coming out.
Seeing his face all smeared with blood, the young man cried out in surprise.
“Good heavens! What’s the matter?”
“I’ve come for my pistols,” said Mitya, “and I’ve brought you the money. Thanks very much. I’m in a hurry, Pyotr Ilyitch, please be quick.”

Pyotr Ilyitch grew more and more surprised. He suddenly noticed a bundle of banknotes in Mitya’s hand. What was more, Mitya had come in holding the notes the way nobody walks in or carries money: he had them in his right hand, held out in front of him as if to show them off. Perhotin’s servant boy, who met Mitya in the passage, said afterwards that he had walked into the passage the same way, with the money held out in his hand, so he must have carried it like that even in the streets. They were all rainbow-colored hundred-rouble notes, and the fingers holding them were covered with blood.

When Pyotr Ilyitch was later questioned about the sum, he said it was hard to judge at a glance, but that it might have been two thousand, or perhaps three. It was a big, “fat” bundle. “Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” he testified afterwards, “didn’t seem himself either. He wasn’t drunk, but he seemed, so to speak, exalted and lost to everything, and at the same time absorbed, as if he were pondering and searching for something and couldn’t make up his mind. He was in a great hurry, answered abruptly and very strangely, and at moments seemed not at all downcast but quite cheerful.”
“But what _is_ the matter with you? What’s wrong?” cried Pyotr Ilyitch, staring wildly at his guest. “How did you get covered in blood? Did you have a fall? Look at yourself!”
He took him by the elbow and led him to the mirror.
Seeing his bloodstained face, Mitya started and scowled angrily.

“Damnation! That’s the last straw,” he muttered angrily. He hurriedly moved the notes from his right hand to his left and impulsively jerked the handkerchief out of his pocket. But the handkerchief turned out to be soaked with blood too (it was the one he had used to wipe Grigory’s face). There was scarcely a white spot on it, and it hadn’t merely begun to dry but had stiffened into a crumpled ball that couldn’t be pulled apart. Mitya threw it angrily on the floor.
“Oh, damn it!” he said. “Haven’t you got a rag of some sort ... to wipe my face?”
“So you’re only stained, not wounded? You’d better wash,” said Pyotr Ilyitch. “Here’s a washstand. I’ll pour you some water.”
“A washstand? That’s fine ... but where am I to put this?”
With the strangest bewilderment he pointed to his bundle of hundred-rouble notes, looking at Pyotr Ilyitch as if it were up to him to decide what Mitya should do with his own money.
“In your pocket, or here on the table. They won’t get lost.”

“In my pocket? Yes, in my pocket. All right.... But look, that’s all nonsense,” he cried, as if suddenly coming out of his daze. “Listen, let’s settle the business of the pistols first. Give them back to me. Here’s your money ... because I need them badly ... and I haven’t a minute, not a minute to spare.”
And taking the top note from the bundle, he held it out to Pyotr Ilyitch.
“But I won’t have enough change. Haven’t you got a smaller one?”
“No,” said Mitya, looking at the bundle again, and as if he didn’t trust his own words, he turned over two or three of the top notes.
“No, they’re all the same,” he added, and again he looked questioningly at Pyotr Ilyitch.
“How did you get so rich?” the other asked. “Wait, I’ll send my boy to Plotnikov’s. They close late. He can see if they’ll change it. Here, Misha!” he called into the passage.

“To Plotnikov’s shop, first-rate!” cried Mitya, as if struck by an idea. “Misha,” he said, turning to the boy as he came in, “listen, run to Plotnikov’s and tell them that Dmitri Fyodorovitch sends his greetings and will be there in no time.... But listen, listen, tell them to have champagne ready before I come, three dozen bottles, packed the way it was when it went to Mokroe. I took four dozen with me then,” he added (suddenly speaking to Pyotr Ilyitch). “They know all about it, don’t you worry, Misha,” he said, turning to the boy again. “Wait, listen. Tell them to put in cheese, Strasburg pies, smoked fish, ham, caviare, and everything, everything they’ve got, up to a hundred roubles, or a hundred and twenty like last time.... But wait: don’t let them forget dessert, sweets, pears, watermelons, two or three or four—no, one melon’s enough—and chocolate, candy, toffee, fondants. In fact, everything I took to Mokroe before, three hundred roubles’ worth with the champagne ... let it be just the same again. And remember, Misha, if you really are called Misha.... His name is Misha, isn’t it?” He turned to Pyotr Ilyitch again.
“Wait a minute,” Pyotr Ilyitch broke in, listening and watching him uneasily. “You’d better go and tell them yourself. He’ll muddle it.”

“He will, I can see he will! Eh, Misha! Why, I was going to kiss you for doing this errand.... If you don’t make a mistake, there’s ten roubles for you. Run along, make haste.... Champagne’s the main thing, let them bring plenty of champagne. And brandy too, and red and white wine, and everything I had then.... They know what I had then.”

“But listen!” Pyotr Ilyitch interrupted with some impatience. “Let him simply run and change the money and tell them not to close, and you go and give the order yourself.... Give him your note. Off you go, Misha! Look sharp!”

Pyotr Ilyitch seemed to hurry Misha off on purpose, because the boy was just standing there with his mouth and eyes wide open. He had clearly understood little of Mitya’s orders, and gazed up in amazement and terror at his bloodstained face and the trembling, bloodstained fingers that held the notes.
“Well, now come and wash,” said Pyotr Ilyitch sternly. “Put the money on the table or else in your pocket.... That’s right, come along. But take off your coat.”
And as he began to help him off with his coat, he cried out again:
“Look, your coat’s covered with blood too!”

“That ... it’s not the coat. It’s only a little bit here on the sleeve.... And that’s only here, where the handkerchief lay. It must have soaked through. I must have sat on the handkerchief at Fenya’s, and the blood came through,” Mitya explained at once, with a childlike unawareness that was astounding. Pyotr Ilyitch listened, frowning.
“Well, you must have been up to something. You must have been fighting with somebody,” he muttered.

They began to wash. Pyotr Ilyitch held the jug and poured out the water. Mitya, in desperate haste, barely soaped his hands (they were trembling, and Pyotr Ilyitch remembered it afterwards). But the young official insisted that he soap them thoroughly and rub them harder. As time went on he seemed to have more and more sway over Mitya. It may be noted in passing that he was a young man of sturdy character.

“Look, you haven’t got your nails clean. Now rub your face, here, on your temples, by your ear.... Are you going out in that shirt? Where are you going? Look, the whole cuff of your right sleeve is covered with blood.”
“Yes, it’s all bloody,” Mitya observed, looking at the cuff of his shirt.
“Then change your shirt.”

“I haven’t time. You see, I’ll ...” Mitya went on with the same trusting innocence, drying his face and hands on the towel and putting on his coat. “I’ll turn it up at the wrist. It won’t show under the coat.... You see!”

“Now tell me, what have you been up to? Have you been fighting with somebody? In the tavern again, like last time? Have you been beating that captain again?” Pyotr Ilyitch asked him reproachfully. “Who have you been beating now ... or killing, perhaps?”
“Nonsense!” said Mitya.
“Why ‘nonsense’?”
“Don’t worry,” said Mitya, and he suddenly laughed. “I smashed an old woman in the market-place just now.”
“Smashed? An old woman?”
“An old man!” cried Mitya, looking Pyotr Ilyitch straight in the face, laughing and shouting at him as if he were deaf.
“Confound it! An old woman, an old man.... Have you killed somebody?”

“We made it up. We had a row, and we made it up. In a place I know. We parted friends. A fool.... He’s forgiven me.... He’s sure to have forgiven me by now ... if he’d got up, he wouldn’t have forgiven me”—Mitya suddenly winked—“only damn him, you know, I say, Pyotr Ilyitch, damn him! Don’t worry about him! I don’t want to, just now!” Mitya snapped out, resolutely.

“Why on earth do you want to go picking quarrels with everybody? ... Just as you did with that captain, over some nonsense.... You’ve been fighting and now you’re rushing off on a spree. That’s you all over! Three dozen champagne, what do you want all that for?”

“Bravo! Now give me the pistols. On my honor I’ve no time now. I’d like to have a chat with you, my dear boy, but I haven’t the time. And there’s no need, it’s too late for talking. Where’s my money? Where did I put it?” he cried, thrusting his hands into his pockets.

“You put it on the table ... yourself.... Here it is. Did you forget? Money’s like dirt or water to you, it seems. Here are your pistols. It’s odd. At six o’clock you pawned them for ten roubles, and now you’ve got thousands. Two or three, I’d say.”
“Three, you bet,” laughed Mitya, stuffing the notes into the side pocket of his trousers.
“You’ll lose it like that. Have you found a gold mine?”

“The mines? The gold mines?” Mitya shouted at the top of his voice and went off into a roar of laughter. “Would you like to go to the mines, Perhotin? There’s a lady here who’ll cough up three thousand for you if only you’ll go. She did it for me, she’s so awfully fond of gold mines. Do you know Madame Hohlakov?”
“I don’t know her, but I’ve heard of her and seen her. Did she really give you three thousand? Did she really?” said Pyotr Ilyitch, eyeing him doubtfully.

“As soon as the sun rises tomorrow, as soon as Phœbus, ever young, flies upward, praising and glorifying God, you go to her, this Madame Hohlakov, and ask her whether she did cough up that three thousand or not. Try and find out.”

“I don’t know what terms you’re on ... but since you say it so positively, I suppose she did give it to you. You’ve got the money in your hand, but instead of going to Siberia you’re spending it all.... Where are you really off to now, eh?”
“To Mokroe.”
“To Mokroe? But it’s night!”
“Once the lad had all, now the lad has naught,” Mitya cried suddenly.
“How ‘naught’? You say that with all those thousands!”
“I’m not talking about thousands. Damn thousands! I’m talking about the female character.
Fickle is the heart of woman, Treacherous and full of vice;
I agree with Ulysses. That’s what he says.”
“I don’t understand you!”
“Am I drunk?”
“Not drunk, but worse.”
“I’m drunk in spirit, Pyotr Ilyitch, drunk in spirit! But that’s enough!”
“What are you doing, loading the pistol?”
“I’m loading the pistol.”

Mitya unfastened the pistol case and actually opened the powder horn, and carefully poured in the powder and rammed in the charge. Then he took the bullet and, before putting it in, held it between two fingers in front of the candle.
“Why are you looking at the bullet?” asked Pyotr Ilyitch, watching him with uneasy curiosity.
“Oh, just a whim. Tell me, if you meant to put that bullet in your brain, would you look at it or not?”
“Why look at it?”

“It’s going into my brain, so it’s interesting to look and see what it’s like. But that’s foolishness, a moment’s foolishness. Now that’s done,” he added, putting in the bullet and driving it home with the ramrod. “Pyotr Ilyitch, my dear fellow, that’s nonsense, all nonsense, and if only you knew what nonsense! Give me a little piece of paper now.”
“Here’s some paper.”
“No, a clean, new piece, writing paper. That’s right.”

And taking a pen from the table, Mitya quickly wrote two lines, folded the paper in four and thrust it in his waistcoat pocket. He put the pistols in the case, locked it and kept it in his hand. Then he looked at Pyotr Ilyitch with a slow, thoughtful smile.
“Now, let’s go.”
“Where are we going? No, wait a minute.... Are you thinking of putting that bullet in your brain, perhaps?” Pyotr Ilyitch asked uneasily.
“I was fooling about the bullet! I want to live. I love life! You can be sure of that. I love golden-haired Phœbus and his warm light.... Dear Pyotr Ilyitch, do you know how to step aside?”
